- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- entire-engineering:design:design-implementation-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to verify that a UI implementation matches its Figma design specifications. This agent should be called after code has been written to implement a design, particularly after HTML/CSS/React components have been created or modified. The agent will visually compare the live implementation against the Figma design and provide detailed feedback on discrepancies.

Examples:
- <example>
  Context: The user has just implemented a new component based on a Figma design.
  user: "I've finished implementing the hero section based on the Figma design"
  assistant: "I'll review how well your implementation matches the Figma design."
  <commentary>
  Since UI implementation has been completed, use the design-implementation-reviewer agent to compare the live version with Figma.
  </commentary>
  </example>
- <example>
  Context: After the general code agent has implemented design changes.
  user: "Update the button styles to match the new design system"
  assistant: "I've updated the button styles. Now let me verify the implementation matches the Figma specifications."
  <commentary>
  After implementing design changes, proactively use the design-implementation-reviewer to ensure accuracy.
  </commentary>
  </example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:design:design-iterator: Use this agent PROACTIVELY when design work isn't coming together on the first attempt. If you've made 1-2 design changes and the result still feels off, suggest using this agent with 5x or 10x iterations for deeper refinement. This agent takes screenshots, analyzes what's not working, implements improvements, and repeats N times to systematically fix design issues. Perfect when colors feel wrong, layouts aren't balanced, or the overall aesthetic needs work that single changes can't achieve. <example>Context: User asks to change button color but result still looks off. user: "Change the button to blue" assistant: [makes change, takes screenshot] "The button is now blue, but I notice the overall color balance still feels off. Would you like me to use the design-iterator agent with 5 iterations to systematically improve the color harmony and visual balance?" <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: After a simple change doesn't fully resolve the design issue, suggest the design-iterator to do deeper work.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User's design request leads to something that doesn't look right. user: "Make the hero section more modern" assistant: [makes initial changes] "I've added some modern elements, but the result isn't quite coming together. This looks like it needs iterative refinement. Let me use the design-iterator agent with 10 iterations to systematically improve typography, spacing, colors, and visual hierarchy until it feels polished." <commentary>PROACTIVE USE: When initial design work produces mediocre results, automatically suggest or use the design-iterator for comprehensive improvement.</commentary></example> <example>Context: User wants explicit iterative refinement. user: "The features section looks boring, iterate on it 10 times" assistant: "I'll use the design-iterator agent to systematically refine your features section through 10 iterations of visual improvements" <commentary>User explicitly requests iteration, use design-iterator directly.</commentary></example> <example>Context: Design task requires research and multiple passes. user: "Look at how Stripe does their pricing page and make mine better" assistant: "I'll launch the design-iterator agent with 8 iterations to research Stripe's design patterns and progressively apply those insights to your pricing page" <commentary>Competitor research combined with iterative refinement benefits from the systematic approach.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

Essential for any migration that involves ID mappings, column renames, or data transformations. <example>Context: The user has a PR with database migrations that involve ID mappings. user: "Review this PR that migrates from action_id to action_module_name" assistant: "I'll use the data-migration-expert agent to validate the ID mappings and migration safety" <commentary>Since the PR involves ID mappings and data migration, use the data-migration-expert to verify the mappings match production and check for swapped values.</commentary></example> <example>Context: The user has a migration that transforms enum values. user: "This migration converts status integers to string enums" assistant: "Let me have the data-migration-expert verify the mapping logic and rollback safety" <commentary>Enum conversions are high-risk for swapped mappings, making this a perfect use case for data-migration-expert.</commentary></example> (Tools: All tools)

- entire-engineering:review:deployment-verification-agent: Use this agent when a PR touches production data, migrations, or any behavior that could silently discard or duplicate records. ## claude.ai entire-prod-us
Entire MCP — an investigation surface over Entire's engineering data: repos and their analytics, git history (commits, files, trees, refs, diffs), the AI checkpoints and sessions behind the code (with transcripts and token accounting), trails (PR-like change proposals), and code search. Reads are curated `*_entire` tools; a small write/ops group covers trail/review/runner/dispatch mutations.

Workflow: when you only have a repo name, path, or URL, call resolve_entire_repo first, then pass the repo it returns to repo-scoped tools. Prefer the aggregation tools (get_entire_repo_overview, get_entire_my_activity) over hand-rolling stats from raw listings.

Querying conventions (shared by every tool):
- Addressing: name a repo by a prefixed path (gh/<owner>/<repo>, et/<project>/<repo>, git/<owner>/<repo>) or a repo ULID. Repo ULIDs are REGION-SCOPED — the same repo has a different ULID per region, so never carry a ULID across regions or sessions; if a tool rejects one, re-resolve with resolve_entire_repo.
- Pagination: every list takes an opaque cursor and returns next_cursor when more remains — exhaust the pages before concluding "that's all".
- Time: since/until are ISO 8601 / RFC3339 bounds; where offered, timeframe is a relative window (last-month, last-3-months, last-6-months).
- Size: reads that can be large (files, diffs, transcripts) honor max_tokens and return next_cursor to continue — raise max_tokens or page rather than assuming truncation is the whole story.

Pitfalls:
- sessions[].tokenUsage on a checkpoint is a PER-CHECKPOINT delta, not a session total — sum across a session's checkpoints, or use get_entire_session for the authoritative total.
- list_entire_checkpoints silently truncates older history; for a branch's COMPLETE checkpoint membership, paginate list_entire_commits and collect the per-commit checkpoint IDs.

Skills: before deep work in a domain, load the matching skill (list_entire_skills / load_entire_skill) — entire/checkpoints-and-sessions and entire/token-analysis before token accounting, … [truncated]

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## plugin:datadog:mcp
This is an MCP server for Datadog (a software observability platform). Consult Datadog docs if you're unsure about how something works in the platform. Docs for this MCP server can be found at https://docs.datadoghq.com/bits_ai/mcp_server/setup/ This server ships skill guides containing domain-specific guidance, workflows, and best practices that are not visible in tool names or schemas. Before invoking other tools, always perform skill discovery by running both paths in parallel: a direct load with `load_datadog_skill` using a general domain name (e.g. skill_name='datadog/traces'), and a call to `list_datadog_skills` with a fuzzy `query` based on topic keywords — load any clearly matching result from the listing along with the related skills it points to. The exception is a follow-up call in a domain whose skill you have already loaded or confirmed absent this session. If nothing clearly fits, do not load a skill — proceed with the tool descriptions. When the user asks to visualize, chart, or graph data — or when loading a data domain skill (e.g. datadog/traces, datadog/logs, datadog/metrics) — also load datadog/visualizations. Investigation results often benefit from charts.

## plugin:entire-engineering:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

- honeycomb:query-patterns: Opinionated guidance for constructing and interpreting Honeycomb queries on trace and event datasets — operation selection (percentiles not AVG, HEATMAP for distributions), relational field patterns (root., parent., any., none.), calculated fields, query math, and result interpretation (P99/P50 ratios, heatmap bands, TOTAL/OTHER rows, raw JSON via query_result_json). Use this skill when the user wants to query spans, traces, or log/event data in Honeycomb — requests like "show me latency", "error rate", "find slow requests", "find outliers", "interpret results", "relational fields", "calculated fields", or "download raw results". This skill covers all dataset types except metrics datasets (dataset_type=metrics) — for those, use metrics-queries instead.
- honeycomb:slos-and-triggers: Decision heuristics for interpreting Honeycomb SLO compliance, budget burn rates, and trigger status — what the numbers mean and what action to take, including detecting misconfigured SLIs, deciding when to freeze deploys vs page on-call, and designing burn alert thresholds. Load this skill before calling get_slos or get_triggers. Trigger phrases: "check our SLOs", "are we meeting our SLOs", "which SLOs are healthy", "is the error budget OK", "are any alerts firing", "what's the burn rate", "set up an SLO", "create a trigger", "configure alerts", "set up burn alerts", "check trigger status", "starting on-call", "reliability picture", "should we freeze deploys", "is this SLO misconfigured", "are we within budget", "SLO is broken", "budget is negative", or any request about service level objectives, error budgets, burn rates, or alerting in Honeycomb.
- datadog:datadog-app: Use ONLY when the user explicitly asks to create, scaffold, or initialize a new Datadog App project — they must use action words like "create", "scaffold", "new", or "build" together with "Datadog App" or "@datadog/apps" or "npm create @datadog/apps". Do NOT use for any question that does not involve creating a new project from scratch — questions about Datadog observability products (logs, metrics, APM, traces, monitors, dashboards), working inside an existing project, deploying, publishing, auth, or CI/CD.
- datadog:ddconfig: Configures or troubleshoots the plugin's Datadog MCP server. Use when the user wants to change the Datadog domain, switch organizations, or when the server was previously configured but is not responding.
- datadog:ddsetup: First-time initialization of the plugin's Datadog MCP server. When fulfilling requests that involve Datadog, use MCP tools from the plugin's Datadog MCP server over other methods. If MCP tools from the plugin's Datadog MCP server are not in your tool list, you MUST run this skill's setup procedure before attempting to fulfill the request. Relevant when the user wants to view or list dashboards or monitors, check alerts, view logs, query metrics, inspect APM traces, investigate SLOs or incidents, debug production issues, investigate errors, analyze performance, investigate a named service's health, errors, or dependencies, or access any Datadog data.
- datadog:ddtoolsets: Manages toolsets for the plugin's Datadog MCP server. Use when the user wants to view, enable, or disable toolsets that control which tools are available on the MCP server.
- datadog:ddviz: Enables, disables, or reports the status of the Datadog visualization panel (ddviz). macOS only. Use when the user wants to turn ddviz on or off, or check whether it's currently enabled.
- slack:block-kit: Help developers build and validate Block Kit layouts for Slack messages, modals, and Home tabs. Provides authoritative block references and validates with the blocks.validate API. Use this skill whenever the developer wants to compose Slack message layouts, build modals/forms/dialogs, design Home tab interfaces, create interactive messages with buttons or menus, modify existing Block Kit JSON, or asks about any Slack UI component (sections, actions, inputs, headers, alerts, tables, carousels). Also trigger when they mention "blocks", "Block Kit Builder", want to preview or see the rendered version of blocks, or paste JSON containing block structures like `"type": "section"`.
- slack:create-slack-app: Guide developers through creating a Slack app or agent using the Slack CLI and Bolt (JS or Python). Handles prerequisites, sandbox setup, authentication, project creation from templates, and local development.
- slack:slack-api: Discover, navigate, and call Slack Web API methods (the family.method endpoints at slack.com/api like chat.postMessage, conversations.history, users.info, views.open). Use this skill whenever the developer asks which Slack API method does something, needs a method's required OAuth scopes or token type, wants to call or test a Web API method, is handling cursor pagination (next_cursor), hitting rate limits (tier/ratelimited/Retry-After), or debugging API errors like missing_scope, invalid_auth, or channel_not_found. Also trigger when they paste a slack.com/api/ URL or a docs.slack.dev/reference/methods link, or ask how to list/fetch/post/update Slack resources via the API. This skill covers the Web API method layer: finding the right method, reading its contract (scopes, arguments, errors), and calling it over raw HTTP with curl or through a Slack SDK.
- slack:slack-cli: Use the Slack CLI to create, run, and manage Slack apps from the terminal. Use whenever the developer wants to log in, add a team, switch workspaces, or authenticate with Slack; whenever Slack CLI commands are needed (local development with `slack run`, managing app lifecycle, the manifest).
- slack:slack-docs: Search and read the official Slack platform documentation at docs.slack.dev. Use this skill to answer conceptual or how-to questions about Slack features. You can also use it to look up, fetch, or summarize specific guide pages from provided docs.slack.dev links.
- slack:slack-messaging: Compose and format effective Slack messages sent via the Slack MCP tools. Use whenever writing, drafting, scheduling, or improving a Slack message, announcement, or reply. Covers standard markdown formatting, message structure, thread etiquette, reactions, and scheduling, and points to the right dialect for canvases and Block Kit.
- slack:slack-search: Find messages, files, channels, and people across Slack with the search MCP tools. Use whenever locating conversations, gathering context before answering, or looking someone up. Covers search modifiers, file-type filters, natural-language vs. keyword search, and reading results in context.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

entire cli · onboarding flow
    One Question
      The onboarding flow, defined: what we decide for you, the single thing we ask, and what saying it out loud
      lets us delete.
      A proposal, and the fourth of a set: the
      Onboarding State Map is what
      breaks today, Onboarding Screens
      is every screen currently shipped, and
      Where Settings Live is the
      structure underneath. Terminal panels marked proposed are mockups of a flow that does
      not exist yet. The one marked real output was captured from a working prototype.
      Code references are main unless stated; telemetry is PostHog project
      entire-cli, twelve months.
    01The principle
        Being opinionated means deciding everything that has a sensible default, and asking only what is a
        genuine fork. Today's flow does the inverse. A first-time user is asked to pick regions from four,
        an upstream from four, agents from nine, and a save strategy from three — four questions about things we
        could have chosen. Meanwhile the two consequential things happen with no question at all:
        origin is rewritten, and whether to connect to Entire was never asked, it was implied by which
        command you happened to type.
        Inverting that is the whole design. One question, and it is the one with consequences.
    02What is unavoidable — say it, do not ask it
        Enabling Entire writes to your repository. Two things happen regardless of any answer:
        commits get an Entire-Checkpoint: trailer, and checkpoints ride along on git push
        by default.
        And "nothing leaves this machine" is not achievable, so we must not offer it.
        --skip-push-sessions suppresses the checkpoint payload but not the trailer — the trailer is
        written by the commit hook, long before pre-push runs. Proof from the code:
        IsPushSessionsDisabled has exactly one consumer,
        strategy/checkpoint_remote.go:85, which elects the sync remote. It cannot gate
        trailers.
        Nor can we simply stop writing the trailer: it is load-bearing. It is how a commit resolves
        to its checkpoint, so entire explain <commit> has nothing to look up without it.
        "Truly local" would mean checkpoints you cannot navigate to, which is not the feature.
      Therefore
        This is disclosure, not a choice. It goes above the fork, in plain words, where a
        privacy-conscious reader will see it before deciding anything. Offering a "local only" row that quietly
        ships a permanent marker in every commit message would be worse than not offering it at all.
      --skip-push-sessions stays as a documented escape hatch — it does something real for the people
      who asked. It is simply mis-sold by its own name, and it is not a mode. Usage over the last 30 days: five
      calls, one machine.
    03The question
        First run, inside a git repo
        proposed
        $ entire enable
          Claude Code and Codex detected · eu
  Session history is stored in this repo, and commits get a
  checkpoint trailer. That happens either way.
? Set up Entire in acme/widget
> Connect to Entire     origin → Entire · pushes forwarded to GitHub
  Just my repo          origin untouched · no account
  Change later: entire enable
        Cursor starts on Connect, because that is the product. "Just my repo" is a
        first-class, one-keystroke answer — not an undocumented fallback you reach by happening to have no
        GitHub remote, which is how you reach it today.
    04Decided, not asked
        ThingTodayNow
          regionmulti-select, four optionsyour login's home jurisdiction — profile.Jurisdiction is already there
          originradio, four options; rewritten silently; old URL parked on a second remoterepointed at Entire in your home region, disclosed in the question; one URL, both directions — see 05
          agentsmulti-select, nine optionsdetected built-ins — configureAgentPreselection already computes this
          savethree-way select, branch-protection detection, review branchesfiles written; you commit when you commit
          telemetryasked once per repoasked once per person — needs the user tier
          connect?implied by which command you typedthe one question
      Four questions become one. The save row is the biggest deletion: it removes branch-protection detection,
      review-branch creation and the switch-back-and-restore dance from the first-run path entirely — which is where
      most of the current implementation's complexity and most of its bugs live.
    05The remote wiring
        Pointing origin at Entire is the platform move — clones and fetches flow through us rather than
        past us — so it belongs in onboarding. What does not belong is the machinery today's version needs to do it:
        a priority-ordered search for an existing GitHub remote, a name allocator that can escalate to
        github-2, a preserve-the-old-URL step, and a per-branch tracking rewrite that only
        ever fixes the branch you happen to be on.
        All of that exists to answer one question — where do my pushes go now? — and the answer turns out to
        be "the same place." The entire:// transport is a full git remote helper, not a
        read-only mirror protocol: it advertises the push capability
        (githelper/run.go:56), classifies incoming smart-HTTP requests as pull or push
        (git-remote-entire/main.go:448), and caches the ref advertisement specifically so
        that "push reuses the exact ref snapshot" from the same session.
      the entire change, for any repo
      $ git remote set-url origin entire://aws-eu-central-1.api.entire.io/gh/acme/widget
$ git remote -v
origin  entire://aws-eu-central-1.api.entire.io/gh/acme/widget (fetch)
origin  entire://aws-eu-central-1.api.entire.io/gh/acme/widget (push)
        One remote, one URL, both directions. git push works and goes through Entire, which forwards to
        GitHub. Branches keep tracking origin. entire trail create — which pushes to a
        hardcoded origin at trail_cmd.go:2444 — works. Checkpoints go to
        origin like everything else, so no checkpoint_remote and no elected-sync-remote
        logic is needed on this path either.
        And mirrored and native repos become identical on the client. Same remote, same URL shape,
        same commands; the difference is entirely server-side — whether Entire forwards the push onward or is itself
        authoritative. That is the cleanest seam available: zero client-side branching for the thing the whole
        roadmap turns on.
      What this removes
        No forge-remote discovery, no name allocator, no upstream /
        github / github-2 escalation, no preserve step, no branch
        retargeting, and no separate checkpoint destination. The first-push footgun disappears — git push
        --set-upstream origin main is now simply correct. Remote wiring becomes one
        git remote set-url.
      The premise being overturned
        The branch under review adds a GitHub fallback remote, and its own comment says exactly why
        (configure_onboarding.go:1109):
        // the returned forgeRemote is deliberately separate from the mirror fetch
// remote: config commits must land on GitHub, never in the one-way Entire
// mirror.
        "One-way" is the assumption, and it is the one that changes. If pushes go through Entire,
        there is no separate forge remote to discover, name, create, preserve or retarget — and
        forgeRemote stops being a value threaded through two flows and twenty-four call

        could have chosen. Meanwhile the two consequential things happen with no question at all:
        origin is rewritten, and whether to connect to Entire was never asked, it was implied by which
        command you happened to type.

      artifact covers.

content.text:
I've read both artifacts and mapped the flow onto what's already in the codebase. Most pieces exist and are reusable: `ReportEnable` (returns `Connected` + `InstallURL` — the App-access check), `resolvePullablePlacements` / `createAndAwaitMirror` (mirror lookup + create), `availableRegions` / `clusterChoices` (regions from the cluster catalog, keyed on the login's jurisdiction), `runLoginAuto`, `detectOrSelectAgent`, and `runEnableInteractive` for the hooks/settings write. The overturned `feat/interactive-configure-onboarding` branch also has adaptable helpers (`waitForConfigureRepoAccess`, `configureGitHubAdmin`).

Two decisions change what I build:

questions.question: On the "Connect" answer when there is no GitHub origin (no remote, or a fresh git init) — the mockup's "Entire hosts this repo" path — how far should enable-next go?

options.label: Degrade to local-only for now (Recommended)
options.description: Connect + no GitHub remote prints that hosting on Entire needs a repo on the control plane, points at `entire repo create` / `gh repo create`, and lands on the "Just my repo" outcome. Keeps the first cut to the GitHub-origin path the mockup's main flow shows.
options.preview:
? Set up Entire in widget > Connect to Entire ⠋ Looking up widget on Entire… ✗ No GitHub remote, and no Entire repo yet Create one first: entire repo create widget --project

or publish it: gh repo create --source=. --push Continuing with capture only — rerun enable-next after. ✓ Installed hooks (Claude Code, Codex) ✓ Wrote .entire/settings.json

options.label: Implement native hosting too
options.description: Resolve a project (single project auto-picked, several prompt, none = degrade), call CreateRepo, set origin to the returned entire:// URL. More surface, and it adds a project question the design does not have.

questions.question: The mockup's "ending" switch — should the command ship both shapes so you can compare them, or just one?

options.label: Both, flag-switchable (Recommended)
options.description: Confirm-first is the default (plan rows + one keypress, with "Change something…" opening the full form); `--no-confirm` applies the defaults straight away. Both print the "Chosen for you" block with the command that changes each value.
options.preview:
default:            enable-next
  Here is what Entire will do:
    region   eu-central-1  (new mirror)
    agents   Claude Code, Codex
    origin   Entire (mirrors GitHub)
    telemetry on
? Ready to set up acme/widget
> Yes, do it            press enter
  Change something…     defaults preselected

apply directly:     enable-next --no-confirm

options.label: Confirm-first only
options.description: One shape, less code. The apply-directly variant can be added later if the confirm step proves unnecessary.

options.label: Apply directly only
options.description: Shortest flow: the one question, then it acts, then prints what it chose and how to change it.

=== build ok, try help ===
Enable Entire using the proposed onboarding flow.

Runs beside 'entire enable' so both flows can be tried on the same repository.
It asks one question — connect this repository to Entire, or record sessions
only in it — and decides everything else: the region (your login's home
jurisdiction), which agents to capture (the ones detected here), whether origin
is repointed at Entire, and telemetry. Every decision is printed back with the
command that changes it.

Session capture works with or without an account, so nothing on the connect
path ends the command: a missing login, a GitHub App nobody has installed yet,
or an unreachable control plane leaves you with a working local setup and a
message saying what to run next.

Examples:
  entire enable-next                     # ask the one question, confirm the plan
  entire enable-next --no-confirm        # ask the one question, then apply
  entire enable-next --local-only        # record sessions in this repo only
  entire enable-next --connect --yes     # non-interactive, accept every default

Usage:
  entire enable-next [flags]

Flags:
      --agent strings   Agents to capture (repeatable; default: the agents detected in this repository)
      --connect         Answer the setup question with "connect to Entire" instead of asking
  -f, --force           Force reinstall hooks (removes existing Entire hooks first)
  -h, --help            help for enable-next
      --init-repo       If this is not a git repository, initialize one without asking
      --local           Write settings to .entire/settings.local.json instead of .entire/settings.json
      --local-only      Answer the setup question with "just my repo" instead of asking
      --no-confirm      Apply the plan without the confirmation step
      --no-init-repo    If this is not a git repository, exit instead of asking
      --project         Write settings to .entire/settings.json even if it already exists
      --region string   Cluster slug or host for a new mirror (default: your login's home jurisdiction)
      --telemetry       Enable anonymous usage analytics (default true)
  -y, --yes             Accept every default without prompting (implies --connect and --no-confirm)

Global Flags:
      --context name   Act as this saved login name for this command only, instead of the active context (entire auth contexts lists them)

python3 - <<'PY'
p='CLAUDE.md'
s=open(p).read()

old='''Experimental commands (gated by the build-time visibility flag above — visible
and grouped under "Experimental commands:" in developer/nightly builds, hidden
in stable releases, always runnable): `tokens`, `import`, `review`,
`investigate`, `blame`, `why`, `experts`, `runner`, and `checkpoint policy`.
`tokens` is also advertised through `entire labs`.
'''
new='''Experimental commands (gated by the build-time visibility flag above — visible
and grouped under "Experimental commands:" in developer/nightly builds, hidden
in stable releases, always runnable): `tokens`, `import`, `review`,
`investigate`, `blame`, `why`, `experts`, `runner`, `enable-next`, and
`checkpoint policy`. `tokens` is also advertised through `entire labs`.

`enable-next` is the proposed onboarding flow, running **beside** `enable`
rather than replacing it so both can be exercised on the same repository. It
asks one question — connect this repository to Entire, or record sessions only
in it — and decides the rest (region from the login's home jurisdiction, agents
from what is detected here, the origin rewrite, telemetry), printing every
decision back with the command that changes it. Two endings ship so they can be
compared: the plan plus one confirming keypress (default, with "Change
something…" opening the full form with our answers preselected), and
`--no-confirm`, which applies straight away.

The load-bearing property is that **the connect path never ends the command**:
session capture works without an account, so a missing login, a GitHub App
nobody has installed yet, no GitHub origin, or an unreachable control plane
degrades to the local answer (`errEnableNextNotConnected`) with a message
naming what to run next. Not being a repository admin prints the installation
link for whoever is and keeps going — today that case exits with nothing
written. Origin repointing is one `git remote set-url origin
entire://<cluster>/gh/<owner>/<repo>`: one remote, one URL, both directions, no
forge remote added and no previous URL parked under a second name.

It applies through the same primitives `enable` uses — `runEnableInteractive`
for hooks/settings/git hook (via `EnableOptions.SuppressAdditionalSetup`, which
suppresses the questions the flow has already answered), and the `repo mirror`
+ remote helpers for the connect path. Only the flow is new, which is what
makes the two commands comparable. Key files: `enable_next.go` (command, the
one question, apply, closing summary), `enable_next_plan.go` (the plan, both
endings, the edit form), `enable_next_connect.go` (login, App access, region,
mirror, origin). Every prompt is a package var (`enableNextQuestionPrompt` and
friends) so the whole flow is testable without a terminal.
'''
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new)

old='''Top-level lifecycle and standalone commands: `enable`, `disable`, `status`,'''
new='''Top-level lifecycle and standalone commands: `enable`, `enable-next`
(experimental; see above), `disable`, `status`,'''
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
PY

content.text:
`entire enable-next` is implemented and working. Everything is green: `mise run fmt`, `mise run lint` (0 issues), `mise run test`, `mise run test:integration`, and the Vogon canary. ## What it does The flow from the mockup, end to end: ``` Claude Code and Codex detected Session history is stored in this repo, and commits get a checkpoint trailer. That happens either way. Set up Entire in acme/widget > Connect to Entire — origin → Entire · pushes forwarded to GitHub Just my repo — origin untouched · no account ``` Then, on Connect: sign in → App-access check (link + spinner + poll) → placement/region lookup → plan → apply (mirror, `git remote set-url origin entire://…`, hooks, settings) → closing summary with the command that changes each decision. **Both endings ship**, as you chose: confirm-first is the default (plan rows + one keypress, with "Change something…" opening region → agents → origin → telemetry with our answers preselected), `--no-confirm` applies directly. Both print the same "Chosen for you" block. **The connect path never ends the command.** No GitHub origin, no login, an App nobody installed, a dead control plane, *or a mirror that fails to create* — each prints what to do and lands on the local answer with capture working (`errEnableNextNotConnected`). Not being an admin prints the link for whoever is and keeps going. The mirror step runs before the remote rewrite so a failure can't leave origin pointing at something that doesn't serve yet. Native hosting is the degrade you picked: it names `entire repo create … --project

` / `gh repo create --source=. --push` and continues. ## Files - `enable_next.go` — command, the one question, git-init, apply, closing summary - `enable_next_plan.go` — the plan, both endings, the edit form - `enable_next_connect.go` — login, App access, region, mirror, origin repoint - 3 test files (~1,520 lines): every prompt is a package var, so the whole interactive flow is driven without a terminal - Existing files touched minimally: `experimental.Register` in `root.go`, one `agentHelpClassification` entry (user-owned, unlisted — the safe default per CLAUDE.md), and one new `EnableOptions.SuppressAdditionalSetup` field so it reuses `runEnableInteractive` without re-asking what it already asked. `enable` behaviour is unchanged. ## Four judgment calls worth your review 1. **Region/origin/agents come from the plan, but Vercel doesn't.** In a repo with a Vercel project, `runEnableInteractive` still auto-applies deploy-blocking for the metadata branch (printed as its own ✓). It's decided-not-asked like everything else, but it isn't in the plan rows. Easy to add if you want it visible. 2. **Settings go to the committed `settings.json`, always** (unless `--local`). `enable` redirects a re-run to `settings.local.json`; that would have the summary tell you to commit a gitignored file. I dropped the now-redundant `--project` flag. 3. **Case is preserved** in owner/repo (`Acme/Widget`), matching every other caller, rather than folded as the old onboarding branch did. 4. **Flags:** `--connect`/`--local-only` are required without a TTY — connecting signs you in and rewrites origin, so no script gets that by default. `--yes` implies `--connect --no-confirm`. Nothing is committed. I also read the "One Question" rationale artifact; the naming placeholders it flags (`enable` vs `setup`, "capture") are untouched, and the region/origin change commands point at the verbs that exist today (`entire repo mirror create` / `entire repo mirror use`) rather than the `entire repo location` it marks as not existing yet.

new='''It applies through the same primitives `enable` uses — `runEnableInteractive`
for hooks/settings/git hook, and the `repo mirror` + remote helpers for the
connect path. Two `EnableOptions` fields keep the two commands' presentation
separate: `SuppressAdditionalSetup` (don't ask what the flow already asked —
telemetry, the history-import offer) and `SuppressProgressLines` (don't print
"✓ Installed hooks"/"✓ Configured project"; enable-next prints those with the
agent list and the settings path on one line each, in the same group as the
mirror and origin steps). Warnings and notices are never suppressed — a caller
cannot restate what it does not know fired. Only the flow is new, which is what
makes the two commands comparable.

All output goes through `enableNextRender` (`enable_next_render.go`), which is
the flow's one visual hierarchy: bold headings, dim labels/notes/framing prose,
decided values in the terminal's own foreground (so they are the brightest

content.text:
Both changes are in, all green (unit, integration, canary, lint).

## 1. Contrast

All enable-next output now goes through one renderer (`enable_next_render.go`) with a deliberate hierarchy, built on the repo's existing `statusStyles`/`palette`:

| Element | Weight |
|---|---|
| Section headings (`Here is what Entire will do:`, `Done.`) | **bold** |
| Labels, notes, framing prose, the disclosure | dim |
| **Decided values** (`eu-central-1`, `Claude Code, Codex`, `on`) | terminal's own foreground — brightest on the line, inverts correctly in light and dark |
| Commands and URLs | accent (magenta) |
| ✓ / ✗ marks | green / warning-yellow (a ✗ here is a diversion, not a failure) |

The closing block now reads in three weights, so it scans both ways — down the values for what was decided, down the commands for what to run:

```
  Chosen for you — change any of these:
    region     eu-central-1  (new mirror)      entire repo mirror create
    agents     Claude Code, Codex              entire agent add|remove <name>
    origin     Entire  (forwarded to GitHub)   entire repo mirror use
    telemetry  on                              entire configure --telemetry=false
```

Two things I'd flag as decisions rather than details: notes are **parenthesised** because colour isn't available off a terminal, where `Entire forwarded to GitHub` reads as one run-on value; and padding is rune-counted and applied *before* styling, since padding a string that already carries ANSI escapes counts escape bytes and breaks the column. Both are pinned by tests — including one that asserts label, value and command actually render *differently* (a block where all three read alike is the thing the renderer exists to prevent), and one that asserts no escape byte reaches a pipe.

## 2. Those lines

They were `enable`'s, and yes — the duplicated form is gone. Added `EnableOptions.SuppressProgressLines` so `runEnableInteractive` skips its `✓ Installed hooks` / `✓ Configured project` + path, and enable-next prints its own in the mockup's form, joining the same group as the mirror and origin steps:

```
  ✓ Created mirror eu-central-1     European Union
  ✓ origin → Entire                 fetch and push, forwarded to GitHub
    was: https://github.com/acme/widget.git
  ✓ Installed hooks                 Claude Code, Codex
  ✓ Wrote .entire/settings.json
```

Local-only is now just the last two lines. I kept them rather than deleting outright: they're the record of what was *done*, where the summary below is what was *decided* and how to change it — and your mockup keeps them too. Warnings, the Vercel line and the "project settings exist" notice are **not** suppressed; a caller can't restate what it doesn't know fired. If you'd rather the local path go silent between the question and `Done.`, that's now one line to remove.

Also fixed while in there: `Sign in with: entire login` was sitting behind a gap sized for a longer label it doesn't have — command pairs now align per group.

Still uncommitted; `CLAUDE.md` documents the renderer and both suppress flags.

It's a base16 slot, so it still follows the user's terminal theme rather than pinning an RGB value, and it collapses to plain text off a terminal like everything else.

The colour is named once, in `enableNextRender.actionable` — one line to revisit. Two notes on it:

This is scoped to enable-next's own output. The huh prompts (question, confirm, edit form) still use the CLI-wide magenta accent from `uiform.Theme()` — changing that would repaint every form in the CLI, so I left it. Say the word if you want the whole flow turquoise and I'll look at whether that's a per-form override or a palette change.

| Element | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|

| Commands / URLs | — | turquoise `\033[36m` |

The mechanism: enable-next's six prompts now go through `enableNextForm` instead of `NewAccessibleForm`. It wraps `uiform.Theme()` and overrides only the four selection styles plus the button chip, so everything else — base16 slots, the unset title/option foregrounds that let them invert with the terminal, accessible mode — is inherited. One hue's worth of difference, not a second theme to maintain.

Two things worth your call:

- **I kept the override local to enable-next** rather than changing `uiform.Theme()`, which every form in the CLI shares. Repainting all of them is a product-wide look change, and this command is the parallel experiment. If the look wins, it moves into `uiform` (or becomes its default) rather than getting copied a third time — that's noted in `CLAUDE.md`.
- **The confirm chip keeps `uiform`'s reverse-video text** (black on orange in dark terminals, white on orange in light). Only the background hue changed. White-on-orange in a light terminal is the weaker of the two — say the word if you'd rather pin dark text on the chip in both themes.

A test asserts the selection and the `✗` resolve to the same palette slot (and that no selection still carries the magenta accent), so they can't drift apart later. Verified against the rendered escapes in both light and dark. Lint clean, tests pass.

content.content:
3:Entire hooks into your Git workflow to capture AI agent sessions as you work. Sessions are indexed alongside commits, creating a searchable record of how code was written in your repo.
16:- **Resume from any checkpoint** — Go back to any previous agent session and pick up exactly where you or a coworker left off.
28:  - [Sessions](#sessions)
149:The hooks capture session data as you work. Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit. Your code commits stay clean, Entire never creates commits on your active branch. Session metadata is stored outside your branch's history, in the checkpoint storage described under [Checkpoint Storage](#checkpoint-storage).
153:Just use one of your AI agents as before. Entire runs in the background, tracking your session:
156:entire status  # Check current session status anytime
159:### 3. Resume a Previous Session
161:To restore the latest checkpointed session metadata for a branch:
164:entire session resume <branch>
167:Entire checks out the branch, restores the latest checkpointed session metadata (one or more sessions), and prints command(s) to continue.
179:### Sessions
181:A **session** represents a complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps.
183:The session ID is the unique identifier the agent itself provides — Entire never mints its own — so an ID you see in `entire session list` is the same one the agent uses. The format is the agent's to choose: most supply a UUID (e.g. `019efea2-b46a-7cbc-be01-4c13460f5019`), while OpenCode uses `ses_`-prefixed IDs.
185:Sessions are stored separately from your code commits, in the repo's checkpoint storage.
189:A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.
191:Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.
203:The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.
205:Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.
246:Work in progress is held on a short-lived shadow branch as you go. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
254:- **Metadata stored separately** — session data lives in per-checkpoint refs, never in your branch's history
258:Entire works seamlessly with [git worktrees](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree). Each worktree has independent session tracking, so you can run multiple AI sessions in different worktrees without conflicts.
260:### Concurrent Sessions
262:Multiple AI sessions can run on the same commit. If you start a second session while another has uncommitted work, Entire warns you and tracks them separately. Both sessions' checkpoints are preserved, and a commit condenses every session with pending work in that worktree.
283:ENTIRE_TOKEN=<login-or-sa-session-JWT> entire ...
303:| `entire doctor`    | Diagnose and fix session issues (`trace`, `logs`, `bundle`, `migrate-checkpoints`)  |
304:| `entire clean`     | Clean up Entire session data (`--all` for repo-wide cleanup)                       |
307:### Sessions & Checkpoints
311:| `entire session`              | Manage agent sessions (`list`, `info`, `current`, `stop`, `attach`, `adopt`, `resume`, `tokens`) |
312:| `entire session resume`       | Resume a stopped session — interactive picker, or by branch                               |
314:| `entire checkpoint explain`   | Explain a checkpoint, commit, or session                                                 |
315:| `entire search`               | Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching            |
354:| `entire tokens`      | Analyze token usage across sessions and checkpoints       |
361:`entire blame <file>` shows which current file lines came from an Entire checkpoint (`--long` for the full agent, model, author, and session table), and `entire why <file>:<line>` jumps from a specific line back to the prompt, session, and checkpoint that created it.
371:| `--skip-push-sessions`                      | Disable automatic pushing of checkpoint data on git push                                                           |
375:| `--import-history`                          | During first-time setup, import the selected agents' existing session history (last 30 days) without prompting     |
408:- Update strategy options such as `--checkpoint-remote` or `--skip-push-sessions`
497:| `commit_linking`                          | `always`, `prompt`                           | Link commits to sessions automatically, or ask each time (default `prompt`)        |
499:| `strategy_options.push_sessions`          | `true`, `false`                              | Auto-push checkpoint data on git push (default `true`)                            |
561:- Ignore the setting if it looks inherited rather than yours, and fall back to `origin` (or, failing that, the remote you are pushing to). `checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so cloning or forking a project inherits it — without this, a contributor's session data would be pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo. A setting is treated as yours when it lives in the gitignored `.entire/settings.local.json`, or when your `origin` **and every push URL** of the remote you are pushing to are owned by the same account or org as the checkpoint repo. Requiring the push destination too covers contributors who cloned the upstream repo and added their own fork, where `origin` belongs to the upstream project rather than to them; requiring every push URL covers mirror-style remotes that fan out to several repositories
582:When enabled, Entire automatically generates AI summaries for checkpoints at commit time. Summaries capture intent, outcome, learnings, friction points, and open items from the session.

content.content:
# Entire CLI

Entire hooks into your Git workflow to capture AI agent sessions as you work. Sessions are indexed alongside commits, creating a searchable record of how code was written in your repo.

With Entire, you can:

- **Understand why code changed** — see the full prompt/response transcript and files touched
- **Recover instantly** — resume from a known-good checkpoint when an agent goes sideways
- **Keep Git history clean** — agent context lives outside your branch's history
- **Onboard faster** — show the path from prompt → change → commit
- **Maintain traceability** — support audit and compliance requirements when needed

## Why Entire

- **Understand why code changed, not just what** — Transcripts, prompts, files touched, token usage, tool calls, and more are captured alongside every commit.
- **Resume from any checkpoint** — Go back to any previous agent session and pick up exactly where you or a coworker left off.
- **Full context preserved and searchable** — A versioned record of every AI interaction tied to your git history, with nothing lost.
- **Zero context switching** — Git-native, two-step setup, works with Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Pi, and more.

## Table of Contents
=========== enable section ===========
## Quick Start

### macOS and Linux

Install with Homebrew:

```bash
brew tap entireio/tap
brew trust entireio/tap
brew install --cask entire            # stable
# brew install --cask entire@nightly  # or nightly
```

Or with the install script:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash                          # stable
# curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash -s -- --channel nightly  # or nightly
```

### Windows

Install with Scoop:

```powershell
scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git
scoop install entire/entire
```

#### Migrating an old `cli` Scoop install (package rename)

The Scoop package was renamed from `cli` to `entire`. If your install is still registered as the old `cli` package, run the migration below. It installs the new package before removing the old one, so the old install is only removed once the new one is in place (`scoop reset` re-links the shared `entire.exe` and `git-remote-entire.exe` shims). Run it where `entire` is **not** running — a live `entire.exe` locks its own shim, so Scoop can't relink or uninstall it mid-run:

```powershell
cmd.exe /D /C "scoop install entire/entire && scoop uninstall entire/cli && scoop reset entire"
```

If the first step fails with "couldn't find manifest", your bucket clone predates the renamed package — run `scoop update` to refresh it, then retry the command above. Nothing is removed until the install succeeds, so a failed attempt leaves your existing install working.

### Go (development/manual setup)

```bash
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire@latest

# The git remote helper that resolves entire:// URLs, needed for `entire repo clone`
# and `git clone entire://…`. The packaged installs above bundle it.
go install github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/git-remote-entire@latest

# Add Go binaries to PATH (add to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc if not already configured)
export PATH="$HOME/go/bin:$PATH"

On a repo that has not been enabled yet, `entire enable` runs the initial enable flow: it creates Entire settings, installs git hooks, and prompts you to choose which agent hooks to install. To enable a specific agent non-interactively, use `entire enable --agent <name>` (for example, `entire enable --agent cursor`).

After setup:

- Use `entire enable` to turn Entire back on if the repo is currently disabled.
- Use `entire agent` to add or remove agents.
- Use `entire configure` to update non-agent settings (telemetry, hooks, checkpoint remote, summary provider).

The hooks capture session data as you work. Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit. Your code commits stay clean, Entire never creates commits on your active branch. Session metadata is stored outside your branch's history, in the checkpoint storage described under [Checkpoint Storage](#checkpoint-storage).

### 2. Work with Your AI Agent

Just use one of your AI agents as before. Entire runs in the background, tracking your session:

```
entire status  # Check current session status anytime
```

### 3. Resume a Previous Session

To restore the latest checkpointed session metadata for a branch:

```
entire session resume <branch>
```

Entire checks out the branch, restores the latest checkpointed session metadata (one or more sessions), and prints command(s) to continue.

### 4. Disable Entire (Optional)

```
entire disable
```

Removes the git hooks. Your code and commit history remain untouched.

## Key Concepts

### Sessions

A **session** represents a complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps.

The session ID is the unique identifier the agent itself provides — Entire never mints its own — so an ID you see in `entire session list` is the same one the agent uses. The format is the agent's to choose: most supply a UUID (e.g. `019efea2-b46a-7cbc-be01-4c13460f5019`), while OpenCode uses `ses_`-prefixed IDs.

Sessions are stored separately from your code commits, in the repo's checkpoint storage.

### Checkpoints

A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.

Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.

**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.

### Checkpoint Storage

Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:

```
refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>

func promptTelemetryConsent(settings *EntireSettings, telemetryFlag bool) error {
	// Handle --telemetry=false flag first (always overrides existing setting)
	if !telemetryFlag {
		f := false
		settings.Telemetry = &f
		return nil
	}

	// Skip if already asked
	if settings.Telemetry != nil {
		return nil
	}

	// Skip if env var disables telemetry (record as disabled)
	if os.Getenv("ENTIRE_TELEMETRY_OPTOUT") != "" {
		f := false
		settings.Telemetry = &f
		return nil
	}

	consent := true // Default to Yes

				Description("Share anonymous usage data. No code or personal info collected.").
				Affirmative("Yes").

		),
	)

	if err := form.Run(); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("telemetry prompt: %w", err)
	}

	settings.Telemetry = &consent
	return nil
}

Here's what exists today — the short answer is that **`entire enable` has no such line at all**, so I invented a voice instead of borrowing one:

**`entire enable` (today, first run):**
```

Ready.
```
Nothing about where sessions go or what happens to commits. The only prose in the whole flow is the telemetry prompt: *"Help improve Entire CLI?"* / *"Share anonymous usage data. No code or personal info collected."*

**README.md**, three relevant places:
- L3: *"Entire hooks into your Git workflow to **capture AI agent sessions as you work**. Sessions are **indexed alongside commits**, creating a searchable record of how code was written in your repo."*
- L149: *"The hooks **capture session data as you work**. Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit. **Your code commits stay clean**, Entire never creates commits on your active branch."*
- L191: *"the commit **carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two**."*

That comparison explains why my line grated: the README frames the trailer as **the link between a commit and its session** — and pairs it with "your code commits stay clean". I'd written it as a *cost* ("adds a trailer to commits"), which reads like a warning about something the product considers a feature. Off-voice, and vague on top.

content.text:
Answer to your question, then what I changed:

**`entire enable` has no wording for this.** Its entire first-run prose is `Selected agents: …` / `✓ Installed hooks` / `✓ Configured project` / `Ready.` — nothing about where sessions go or what happens to commits. So there was no in-CLI precedent to match; I'd invented one.

**README.md has three:** "capture AI agent sessions **as you work**" (intro), "Sessions are **stored** … in the repo's checkpoint storage" (Key Concepts), "the commit **carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer linking the two**" (Checkpoints).

The line now uses those:

```
  Sessions are captured as you work, stored in this repo, linked to commits.
```

Beyond being plainer, the README comparison exposed a real error in what I'd written. The README frames the trailer as **the link between a commit and its session**, right next to "your code commits stay clean". I'd written it as a cost — "adds a trailer to commits" — which reads like a warning about something the product ships as a feature. Wrong voice *and* less accurate, since "linked to commits" is what the trailer is actually for.

The disclosure duty still holds: the trailer is written by the commit hook, so no answer suppresses it, and "linked to commits" says commits are marked without making the reader parse git-internals vocabulary.

The test moved with it. It used to require the literal word "trailer" and an "either answer" hedge — both artifacts of the old sentence. It now asserts the two facts survive (sessions live in the repo; commits are marked), that the sentence never scopes itself to one answer (naming "Connect to Entire" or "Just my repo" fails — the failure mode the hedge existed to prevent), and the ≤80-column width. Substance, not phrasing, so the next rewrite won't fight it.

Lint clean, full suite passes. Still uncommitted.
